subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: verifying AI answers against sources [Action]
passage:
In the school library, Trisha typed her history question into an AI tool: when did the Battle of Plassey take place? It answered 1758 in confident, neat sentences. She began copying it into her notes, then paused. The textbook was on the desk. She flipped to chapter six: 1757. She checked the index, then the timeline on page 84. Both said 1757. Ramesh Sir, the librarian, passed with a trolley and glanced over. “Something wrong?”
“The AI gave me a different date from the book.”
“Which do you trust for an exam?”
“The book. And I should confirm with a second source. It can make mistakes.”
She crossed out 1758, wrote 1757 with a star, and added at the top of the page: AI is a starting point, not the final answer.

qa.q: What date did the AI give?
How does Trisha feel about the AI after finding the error?
qa.a: Trisha feels wary and more careful, since she now treats the tool as fallible and wants a second source.

qa.q: What could Trisha do to check other facts?
qa.a: Trisha could compare the textbook, its index and timeline, or ask a teacher or the librarian, since reliable sources can confirm a claim.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Sir see what Trisha did?
qa.a: Ramesh Sir is probably pleased that a student checked, and his question about which she trusts invites her to use her own reasoning.

grounding: A student checks a historical date the AI gave against the textbook, finds an error and learns to treat the tool as fallible.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: verifying AI answers against sources [Action]
passage:
Dear Hafsa,
You'll laugh at this. Last week I was revising for the history test and asked an AI tool for a quick timeline of the Revolt of 1857. It gave me a neat list, and one line said the Doctrine of Lapse was introduced in 1868. Something itched. I opened our textbook, and the chapter clearly said it was applied in the late 1840s and early 1850s, before the revolt. Which makes sense, because it was one of the causes! The AI's date put the cause after the effect.
I asked the tool again, and it apologised and corrected itself, which almost made it worse. How many other lines had I just believed?
So now I have a rule: the AI can give me a starting point, but every date and name gets checked in the textbook or another proper source before it goes into my notes.
Write back soon and tell me how your exams are going.
Love,
Swati

qa.q: What date did the AI give for the Doctrine of Lapse?
qa.a: It said it was introduced in 1868.

qa.q: How did Swati feel after the AI corrected itself?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy, even more worried than before, wondering how many other lines had been believed without checking.

qa.q: What else could Swati do when two sources disagree?
qa.a: Swati could check a third reliable source or ask the history teacher, rather than trusting whichever answer sounds most confident.

qa.q: How might Hafsa react to the letter?
qa.a: Hafsa might laugh at the story but also start checking any AI answers, having seen how easily a wrong date slips in.

grounding: Shows a student checking an AI-given historical date against the textbook, finding an error and deciding to confirm claims from reliable sources.

passage: So you asked me, Lakshmi, why I'm so fussy about checking now. Okay. I'm Baljeet, and this is my confession. Before the Class 9 history quiz, I asked an AI tool for the year of the Battle of Plassey. It said 1764, very confidently. I wrote it on my flashcard. Two days later, you remember, you were reading the textbook aloud on the bus, and you said 1757. I said, "No, the AI said 1764." You opened the page and showed me. 1757. And 1764 was Buxar, a different battle. The tool had mixed up two battles. I felt so stupid, and also a bit shocked, because it had sounded so sure. Now every date from a tool goes into my notes only after I've found it in the textbook. Sounding sure and being right are not the same thing.

qa.q: What year did the AI give for the Battle of Plassey?
How did Baljeet feel when the textbook showed 1757?
qa.a: Baljeet felt stupid and a bit shocked that the AI had sounded so sure while being wrong.

qa.q: What else could Baljeet do to catch such errors before a quiz?
qa.a: Baljeet could check each flashcard against the textbook the day it is made, instead of waiting for a friend to spot a mistake.

qa.q: How was Lakshmi part of catching the mistake?
qa.a: Lakshmi, reading the textbook aloud on the bus, caught the wrong date and showed the page, helping Baljeet see that the tool can be wrong.

grounding: Illustrates a student finding that an AI mixed up a historical date, confirmed by the textbook, and learning to verify claims from reliable sources.
